title: Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Communication Layers

hero.subtitle: The definitive requirements specification for Internet host software implementations

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1122 defines the requirements for the software of Internet hosts on the communication protocol layers: link layer, IP layer, and transport layer. It is a cornerstone document that established the conventions for how Internet standards express requirements.

This RFC introduced the now-ubiquitous MUST, SHOULD, MAY, MUST NOT, and SHOULD NOT requirement levels that were later formalized in RFC 2119. These terms have become the standard language for all Internet specifications.

MUST / MUST NOT
Absolute requirement. An implementation that does not satisfy a MUST requirement is non-conformant.
SHOULD / SHOULD NOT
Strong recommendation. There may be valid reasons to deviate, but the implications must be understood.
MAY
Truly optional. An implementation may include or omit this feature.

sections.title: Link Layer
sections.content:
The link layer requirements cover how hosts interface with the physical network:

ARP Implementation
Hosts MUST implement ARP for address resolution on broadcast networks. The ARP cache SHOULD include a mechanism for flushing stale entries and MUST support dynamic updates.
Trailer Encapsulation
Hosts MUST NOT send trailer-encapsulated packets unless the recipient has negotiated trailer use. This deprecated feature moved protocol headers after the data in Ethernet frames.
Maximum Transmission Unit
The link layer MUST provide a way for the IP layer to determine the MTU of the link. Ethernet has a standard MTU of 1500 bytes.

sections.title: IP Layer
sections.content:
IP layer requirements cover addressing, routing, fragmentation, and ICMP handling:

ReassemblyMUST be able to reassemble fragments up to 576 bytes; SHOULD handle larger
TTLMUST set the TTL to a reasonable value (default suggested: 64)
Source RouteMUST be able to receive and forward source-routed packets
ICMPMUST support generating and processing ICMP error and info messages
BroadcastMUST recognize and handle limited and directed broadcasts

The "Robustness Principle" (Postel's Law) is emphasized: "Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send." This principle has guided Internet protocol design for decades.

sections.title: Transport Layer
sections.content:
Transport layer requirements cover both TCP and UDP:

TCP Requirements
Hosts MUST implement TCP. TCP MUST implement: urgent data, Nagle algorithm (SHOULD be enabled by default), delayed ACKs (no more than 500ms), Karn's algorithm for RTT estimation, and congestion avoidance.
UDP Requirements
Hosts MUST implement UDP. Applications SHOULD verify the UDP checksum on received datagrams. The UDP checksum MUST be computed on transmitted datagrams when possible.
Port Assignment
Well-known ports (0-1023) are reserved for standard services. Hosts MUST support ephemeral ports for client connections, typically in the range 49152-65535.
TCP Feature
Requirement Level
Delayed ACKs
SHOULD (max 500ms delay)
Nagle Algorithm
MUST implement, SHOULD enable by default
Keep-Alive
MAY implement (default OFF, interval >= 2 hours)
Urgent Data
MUST implement
RST on Closed Port
MUST send RST

sections.title: Application Layer
sections.content:
While RFC 1122 focuses on communication layers, it includes guidance for how applications interact with the transport layer:

Interface Requirements
The host MUST provide a programming interface (API) that allows applications to: open/close connections, send/receive data, set TTL and TOS values, and be notified of errors.
Error Reporting
Transport and IP layer errors (ICMP messages, connection resets) SHOULD be reported to the application. The application should be able to handle these errors gracefully.
Multihoming
A host with multiple IP addresses MUST allow applications to specify which source address to use for outgoing connections.

RFC 1122 is complemented by RFC 1123 (Host Requirements - Application and Support), which covers application-layer protocols such as Telnet, FTP, SMTP, and DNS.

references.text: Braden, R., "Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Application and Support", RFC 1123, October 1989.
Bradner, S., "Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels", RFC 2119, March 1997.
